name: 100% network-upgrade cost
desc: Make large loads pay 100% of the network upgrades they trigger; DOE asked about a crediting mechanism.

letters.desc: The filing supports assigning 100 percent of attributed network upgrade costs to the interconnecting load, consistent with generator interconnection rules. Any crediting mechanism should be limited to upgrades that provide general system-wide benefit, not used to subsidize large loads at ratepayer expense.
quotes: United encourages aligning cost responsibility for load interconnection with cost responsibility for generator interconnection. In that vein, it is logical that both load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades they are attributed to serve the load.
Should the Commission adopt a crediting mechanism to offset costs, this should only be applied to the extent that the network upgrades are shown to bring general benefit to load.

letters.desc: ACORE ties lower network upgrade costs to joint study and accelerated deployment of grid enhancing technologies, high-performance conductors, and an enumerated list of alternative transmission technologies.
quotes: Essential to cost-effectively meeting the large load needs is an accelerated deployment of Grid Enhancing Technologies and High-Performance Conductors.
ACORE agrees with the ANOPR recommendations to study load and hybrid facilities together with generating facilities as a means to improve the process efficiency and lower network upgrade costs

One gap in the ANOPR principles that should be incorporated into a rulemaking on the interconnection of large loads is to mirror Order No. 2023’s requirements for “transmission providers to evaluate the following enumerated list of alternative

letters.desc: AEP opposes direct assignment of 100% of network upgrade costs to large load customers and favors rolled-in rate treatment consistent with longstanding Commission precedent. Proper cost allocation also ensures transmission owners earn a lawful return to attract investment capital.
quotes: To protect other customers, large loads must pay their fair share for the transmission system expansion needed to serve them, and the Commission also needs to fundamentally reconsider how generator interconnection and transmission system planning are conducted to ensure that reforms drive cost-effective development to support interconnecting loads.

AEP agrees with commenters arguing that network upgrade costs for large load interconnections should be rolled into transmission rates and that direct assignment of 100% of such network upgrade costs to large load customers is not appropriate.
This is critical to ensure that transmission owners can continue to attract the capital necessary to develop the transmission infrastructure needed to support the interconnection of large loads.

Proactive, multi-value planning is also crucial to foster the development of Extra High Voltage ('EHV') facilities—the essential backbone of the nation's transmission system—because it looks ahead to identify regional and interregional needs and the corresponding EHV solutions.

letters.desc: American Terawatt proposes that an up-front premium paid by developers for accelerated interconnection cover the associated costs, so existing consumers do not bear short-term rate increases.
quotes: By charging a predetermined up-front premium for this form of accelerated interconnection, utilities need not incur increased rates for consumers in the short term.

letters.desc: Buckeye supports direct assignment of 100% of network upgrade, interconnection facility, and attachment facility costs to large loads. It notes that any crediting mechanism must be designed differently from the generator-interconnection financing model to actually prevent cost shifts to other wholesale customers.
quotes: If a large load fails to materialize or consume electricity at the level and duration expected when these transmission investments were made, other wholesale transmission customers (and, ultimately, their retail customers) may be faced with the massive costs of investments they did not cause.

Buckeye supports holding large loads such as data centers directly responsible for 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned through interconnection studies (which could include crediting, provided that crediting is designed to ensure that wholesale transmission customers are protected).

If the relevant wholesale transmission entity, like AEP Ohio, were responsible for the network upgrade costs caused by their retail customers seeking large load interconnections, that could both protect other wholesale transmission customers and still allow a mechanism for ultimately holding large loads responsible for the costs they cause.
An appropriate crediting mechanism for this purpose will need to be different from the crediting mechanism used for large generator interconnections.

letters.desc: Buckeye supports requiring data centers to pay 100% of network upgrade costs upfront, viewing direct assignment as the only approach that reliably prevents stranded cost risk for other ratepayers. A usage-based crediting mechanism can address and-pricing concerns without undermining this protection.
quotes: Large loads, particularly data centers, are driving historic investments in the transmission grid, which have the very real risk of creating significant cost shifts if the large loads do not show up to pay for this investment on a sustained basis.

Direct assignment of upfront costs is the only approach that ensures other ratepayers are not left holding the bag if a large load does not show up on a sustained basis to pay for the investments it has caused.

Rolled-in approaches would force other customers to bear costs they did not cause and expose them to significant stranded cost risk. That is particularly inappropriate given the unique scale, pace, and cost shift risks associated with large data center interconnections.
"and" pricing concerns should not deter the Commission from requiring upfront funding by data centers of the transmission additions they cause.

Crediting would provide the large data center with the opportunity to receive full credits for its upfront payments to the extent that it has sufficient usage over a sustained period of time, thereby protecting other wholesale customers from bearing stranded costs.
The approach of reflecting retail-level solutions in Commission-jurisdictional rates (Part II.C.ii above) should be applied to any large data centers already being studied for interconnection.

letters.desc: Buckeye supports requiring large loads to pay 100% of the network upgrade costs they cause, calling it the most direct and protective approach. If direct assignment is not adopted, Buckeye proposes holding the serving wholesale entity responsible so it can recover costs through retail arrangements with the large load.
quotes: To best protect other customers, the Commission should require large loads to be responsible for 100% of the network upgrade costs they cause.

Buckeye supports the ANOPR's proposal to hold large loads 100% responsible for the network upgrade costs they cause, which is the most protective and direct way to ensure that other customers are protected against the unique and significant risks posed by these large loads.

FERC could hold the relevant wholesale transmission entity with the direct relationship to the large load responsible for large load-driven network upgrade costs, as that entity would be in a position to pass these costs onto the large load under its retail arrangements.
Data centers have likely caused over $24 billion in RTEP projects so far.

letters.org: California Department of Water Resources State Water Project
letters.desc: DWR supports assigning 100% of network upgrade costs to the large loads that trigger them, paired with a crediting mechanism different from the generator model. The mechanism must require actual usage to materialize before credits are earned, to deter speculative requests.
quotes: Unlocking the curtailability of existing loads requires no upgrades or increased ratepayer costs—it simply requires new market functionality.
New large interconnections should finance 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned through the interconnection study process.
If massive transmission investments are made to serve these loads, yet the expected demand does not materialize, other customers may be left holding the bag.

This assignment of costs should be paired with an appropriate crediting mechanism. This crediting mechanism might vary from region-to-region, but it must be designed to keep wholesale customers whole and disincentivize speculative load that will impose costs on wholesale customers.
Such a guaranteed crediting mechanism should not be adopted for large load interconnections because these credits are not tied to particular levels of usage.

letters.desc: The Center supports requiring large-load customers to pay 100% of the network upgrade costs they trigger, and wants the Commission to extend that protection to stranded-asset exposure as well.
quotes: the Commission should adopt clear rules preventing any cost-shifting of network upgrades or stranded assets attributable to large-load customers.

Because data centers both cause and benefit from these upgrades, the Commission must rigorously enforce Principle 8. This includes conducting transparent load interconnection studies and requiring large-load customers to cover 100% of their network upgrade costs, while also strengthening the principle to ensure ratepayers are protected from any stranded-asset costs.

letters.desc: EDF agrees large loads should bear 100% of network upgrade costs assigned through interconnection studies, and notes that joint study of co-located generation can reduce what those costs are. EDF also supports a crediting mechanism for loads whose presence reduces overall transmission rates.
quotes: It is appropriate for large loads and hybrid facilities to pay for network upgrades required for their interconnection and transmission service based on their rights-based interconnection obligations.  As noted above, hybrid facilities should be able to benefit from reduced network upgrade costs by studying co-located generation and load together.

letters.desc: ELCON endorses the cost causation principle: large loads pay for the network upgrades their connections require. The Commission should pair that obligation with flexible crediting mechanisms and an option for the load to self-build required upgrades, easing pressure on utility capital budgets.
quotes: ELCON agrees with principle eight that load be responsible for any necessary network upgrades necessary to connect their facilities to the grid.

We ask that the Commission provide flexibility in the financial and crediting mechanisms to pay for those upgrade costs as well as provide the option to build those upgrades as set out in principle nine.

letters.desc: ECA supports the principle that large load and hybrid customers pay for 100% of assigned network upgrades, consistent with generator interconnection rules. It also endorses crediting mechanisms so other benefiting customers share costs originally assigned to the large load.
quotes: ECA supports measures that ensure that all customers pay for the costs they cause and for the benefits they receive. A guideline requiring load and hybrid facilities to pay for 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned is sensible on its face and consistent with how generators are treated.

letters.desc: Emerald AI supports tying upgrade cost responsibility to flexibility performance: inflexible loads bear upgrade costs while flexible loads avoid them. It frames software-based flexibility as a low-cost substitute for capital-intensive transmission, protecting ratepayers from unnecessary socialization of those costs.
quotes: the marginal cost of software-based flexibility is near-zero (operating expense), whereas the marginal cost of new transmission capacity is extremely high (capital expense).

projects that remain inflexible proceed through the standard process and may bear upgrade-related costs, whereas projects that commit to and deliver flexibility can avoid or reduce those upgrades and connect sooner.

letters.desc: ENGIE agrees that large load and hybrid facilities should bear 100% of network upgrade costs allocated to them and opposes a crediting mechanism that could shift costs to ratepayers. It distinguishes local-benefit upgrades from system-benefit upgrades, which should be socialized.
quotes: ENGIE does not believe that a crediting mechanism is necessary as large load and hybrid interconnection costs should be paid for by the facilities themselves. A credit mechanism may risk shifting costs onto ratepayers.

letters.desc: Entergy insists that large loads must pay the full cost of transmission upgrades they cause, with states retaining jurisdiction over retail cost allocation questions.
quotes: the Commission must not impose any rules that could result in large loads paying less than their fair share of transmission costs, which includes the costs that they cause as a result of the need for upgrades or other appropriate transmission system modifications so that these new loads can be safely and securely interconnected.

letters.desc: ELPC endorses requiring large-load applicants to bear the incremental transmission upgrade and extension costs their connections require. Evidence from PJM shows $4.1 billion in socialized connection costs in 2024 alone, and state commissions in California and Kansas have already moved to direct cost assignment.
quotes: large load customers often require new lines and substations at voltages of 138kV or higher. Mr. Jacobs explained that although such high-voltage connection facilities are essentially line extensions that the utility designs to serve a specific customer, the utilities socialize their costs by placing them into the transmission rate base.
Mr. Jacobs provided his analysis showing that such connection facilities added up to $4.1 billion across PJM in 2024 alone, with costs continuing to increase in 2025 and beyond.

the California Public Utilities Commission recently issued an interim order requiring new transmission-level customers seeking retail services to be responsible for the initial costs of all transmission facilities, rather than those costs being borne by ratepayers.

the Commission should order ComEd to collect deposits for the incremental costs of Large Demand Project Applicants or Customers, regardless of whether those costs are deemed by ComEd to be transmission costs or distribution costs.

letters.desc: Eolian supports extending the option to build to large load interconnection customers and urges greater standardization, cost reporting, and auditability to overcome the barriers that currently make this option difficult to access in practice.
quotes: The Commission should build upon its experience in the generator interconnection process by further reducing barriers to use of the option to build.

letters.desc: ETX takes the position that large loads, hybrids, and co-located facilities should bear 100% of network upgrade costs. It opposes offset or crediting mechanisms that reward co-location when the project has not actually reduced upgrade costs.
quotes: Load, Hybrid and/or co-located load and generation facilities should be responsible for 100% of their network upgrade costs.
If a project cannot achieve that through lower network upgrade costs, it should not be incentivized to do so with an off-set crediting mechanism.

letters.desc: Fervo supports cost-allocation rules that recognize when project design reduces system impact, rather than applying standardized costs that do not reflect actual system benefits or reflect net flows.
quotes: Fervo supports clear cost-allocation rules but emphasizes that any cost-allocation framework must recognize when a project's design meaningfully reduces its system impact.

Hybrid geothermal facilities that "bring their own power" can substantially decrease the need for upstream transmission reinforcements by co-locating firm, dispatchable generation with load, often avoiding or minimizing upgrades that a stand-alone load would otherwise require.

Fervo therefore encourages the Commission to ensure that cost responsibility is applied in a way that reflects actual system benefits and not over-assign costs to hybrids that reduce net flows or improve local reliability.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy supports rolled-in rates and argues that, at minimum, any cost assignment approach must preserve the transmission owner's right to earn a reasonable return on network upgrade investments.
quotes: if the Commission were to impose a requirement that 100% of network upgrade costs appear on a particular retail customer's electricity bill, that would arguably improperly usurp the states' jurisdiction over retail sales
mandating direct assignment will likely lead to the same inefficiencies that have plagued the generator interconnection process, such as numerous withdrawal and restudy cycles

The best way to avoid these pitfalls is to use the Commission's long-standing approach that network upgrade costs are rolled in to the transmission owner's rate base and recovered from all wholesale transmission customers proportionally to their load

letters.desc: FirstEnergy addresses how the substantial network upgrades a single data center requires would be recovered. The expansion rate is designed specifically to recover the cost of those upgrades from the customer driving them, separate from the existing zonal rate that covers the legacy system.
quotes: The agreement would obligate the data center customer to pay two distinct rate components. First, the customer would pay its standard pro-rata share of the existing zonal transmission rate, applying the same tariff structure applicable to all transmission customers within the zone. Second, the customer would pay an expansion rate specifically designed to recover the costs of the network upgrades required to support the interconnection.

letters.org: Georgia Power CompanyAlabama Power CompanyMississippi Power Company ,
letters.desc: The filer reports that large load customers in the Southeast accept paying their share of generation and transmission upgrade costs in exchange for timely service. A proposed federal cost allocation standard for retail customers would duplicate, and potentially override, this working state-level approach.
quotes: large load customers acknowledge the demands they place on existing infrastructure and are willing to pay their share of generation and transmission costs in exchange for timely service.

the eighth reform principle, which suggests a new federal standard for how transmission costs should be allocated to large load retail customers, risks directly intruding on retail ratemaking in jurisdictions that have retained bundled retail service.

letters.desc: GridStor addresses how the costs of network upgrades needed for ESR charging should be handled, recommending they follow the established interconnection cost-allocation framework rather than a separate treatment.
quotes: Such upgrades would be allocated following the established cost-allocation principles applied to other interconnection upgrades.

letters.desc: The filing supports directly assigning network upgrade costs to large-load customers while also charging the NITS rate, following the generator interconnection model from Order No. 2003. It presents four variants: credit upgrade payments against NITS charges, issue interconnection rights in exchange for upgrade payments, apply disaggregated pricing, or clarify that a rate below both is unjust and unreasonable.
quotes: Because the NITS rate does not recover from the large-load customer the costs its interconnection directly imposes on other ratepayers, ratepayers initially subsidize the large-load customer.
If the large-load customer paying the NITS rate departs the system before the crossover point, the only cost shift that would have materialized runs from ratepayers to the large-load customer.
Despite relying on the network, the large-load customer pays nothing for its ongoing development, replacement, maintenance, or operations.
Payments for network upgrades and the NITS rate, the Commission concluded, were two 'separate charges for separate services.'
Under either approach, the utility would directly assign network upgrade costs to the large-load customer and charge the NITS rate.

After the Commission modifies its transmission pricing policy to exempt large-load customers from the prohibition against 'and' pricing, the Commission could find that any transmission rate charging a large-load customer less than the cost of network upgrades and the NITS rate is unjust and unreasonable.

The Commission should extend that reasoning and clarify that just and reasonable rates for large-load customers must recover both the customer-specific interconnection costs and the customer's share of the embedded system.

letters.desc: Heron asks RTOs and transmission owners to credit the grid services of grid-forming loads against direct-assignment network upgrade costs, treating avoided synchronous condensers or flicker devices as a quantifiable benefit to the system.
quotes: the Commission should direct RTOs and transmission owners to credit the grid services provided by grid-forming large loads against any direct-assignment network upgrade costs.
The cost-causation principle underlying ANOPR Principle 8 should apply symmetrically to benefits as well as costs.

letters.desc: The filing argues all upgrade costs should be borne exclusively by the large load through a Contribution in Aid of Construction payment, which keeps the cost-causer responsible, avoids socialization, and eliminates the collection risk that a crediting mechanism creates over the life of an upgrade.
quotes: The costs of large load, hybrid facilities, and associated generation should be paid exclusively by the large load seeking to connect to the system.

Requiring a large load customer to pay all installation and upgrade costs ensures that the cost-causer pays for the system upgrade. This prevents socialization of system costs that do not benefit the breadth of ratepayers and prevents stranding the costs of the upgrade if the customer's business fails.
when customers pay the full cost that they impose on the system through a CIAC payment, it is not necessary to use a crediting mechanism to cover those costs.

letters.desc: The filer insists that transmission owners must earn a reasonable rate of return on all network upgrade assets, citing Hope, Bluefield, and Ameren. Placing such assets in rate base at zero return would chill capital investment, create asymmetric risk, and violate constitutional requirements. As data-center-driven load growth accelerates, the volume of uncompensated upgrades would become unsustainable.
quotes: Costs of transmission network upgrades triggered by interconnection of large load customers should, by default, be rolled into transmission rates consistent with longstanding Commission precedent on the treatment of integrated transmission facilities, rather than directly assigned to individual customers.

Rolled-in rate treatment will promote more efficient and timely large load interconnection by avoiding cost allocation and jurisdictional disputes, as well as ensuring that all load customers continue to contribute their fair share of the benefits of an integrated transmission network.

it would be contrary to law and practically untenable for transmission owners to construct, operate, and maintain these facilities, while taking on the associated risks, without the facilities going into the transmission owners' rate base on which they are allowed to earn a reasonable return.
Under Hope, rates must, at a minimum, 'enable the company to operate successfully, to maintain its financial integrity, to attract capital, and to compensate its investors for the risks assumed.'

the Commission should use that jurisdiction to require that costs benefiting the transmission network be rolled into the transmission providers' rate base and recovered, with a reasonable rate of return, from all network transmission customers.

letters.desc: Hopkins asks FERC to assign transmission upgrade costs to the large loads whose interconnection requires those upgrades, ending the practice of socializing those costs across existing residential ratepayer classes.
quotes: require that large loads, specifically data centers and other high-density commercial facilities, bear the full cost of transmission infrastructure required to interconnect them to the interstate transmission system, rather than socializing those costs across existing ratepayer classes.

letters.desc: iMasons takes no position on whether network upgrade costs should be directly assigned or rolled into rate structures, but insists that whatever method is used must ensure large load customers pay only their fair share of caused costs.
quotes: iMasons encourages the Commission to promulgate a final rule that would require large load customers to be allocated only costs that they cause, consistent with the Commission's longstanding cost causation principles.

letters.desc: IECA supports the applicant-pays principle, requiring Data Centers and associated generators to bear 100% of network upgrade costs, with a crediting mechanism mirroring existing generator interconnection rules.
quotes: we support requiring load and hybrid facilities, including any associated electric generating facilities not sharing an interconnection point with its associated Data Center, to bear all the costs of network upgrades required for their interconnection(s) and we support offsetting such costs through a crediting mechanism as is applicable under the Commissions interconnection rules applicable to generators.

letters.org: Invenergy Wind Development North America LLCInvenergy Solar Development North America LLCInvenergy Thermal Development Holdings LLC ,
letters.desc: Invenergy agrees that large load and hybrid facilities should be allocated 100% of the network upgrade costs they cause, consistent with the cost-causation principle. Hybrid projects should be studied as one unit by default so that cost allocation reflects the net grid impact of co-located load and generation.
quotes: Invenergy agrees with DOE's proposal to make load and hybrid facilities responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through any interconnection studies, rather than allocate such costs to non-large load customers or generators in the interconnection queue.
hybrid projects should be studied as one project for purposes of assigning network upgrade costs, rather than studying the load and generation separately.

letters.desc: ISO-NE agrees that loads and hybrid facilities should bear 100% of interconnection upgrade costs, a construct already in place for RNS in New England. It asks that any crediting mechanism be kept simple.
quotes: ISO-NE agrees with the principle that load and hybrid facilities should be fully responsible for upgrades needed to support their interconnections.  This construct exists today for RNS.  The methodology used to assign responsibility for upgrades and any crediting mechanism should be simple.

letters.desc: LPPC strongly supports assigning 100% of network upgrade costs to large load with no credits or refunds, arguing that credits would shift costs to existing customers who do not benefit from new load as they do from new generation.
quotes: LPPC agrees that load and hybrid facilities should be fully responsible for network upgrades. No credits or refunds should be required, consistent with the principle of assessing costs to cost causers. Large load interconnections of the magnitude contemplated in many parts of the nation hold the potential for substantial cost shifts to existing load.

letters.desc: The comment describes requirements that large load customers pay upfront for dedicated substations, distribution upgrades, and transmission lines so the upgrades needed to serve them do not fall on existing ratepayers.
quotes: Requires the large load customer to pay upfront for dedicated substations, distribution upgrades, transmission lines, and other required facilities.

letters.desc: LS Power supports the beneficiary-pays principle: the large-load customer bears full cost responsibility for any network upgrades triggered by its interconnection. The company also calls for just and reasonable compensation for transmission owners required to own and maintain those facilities, citing Ameren Services Co. v. FERC.
quotes: when a new large load requires system or network upgrades, the new large load customer should bear ultimate cost responsibility consistent with cost causation and beneficiary pays principles.

Attracting the long-term capital needed to meet the infrastructure needs created by the surge in large-load demand requires that all infrastructure investments receive just and reasonable compensation, established to the maximum possible extent through independent planning and competition.

letters.org: Maine Office of the Public Advocate
letters.desc: Maine OPA supports assigning 100% of network upgrade costs to the large load facilities causing them, rejecting any offsets or credits.
quotes: load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through interconnection studies.

letters.org: Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General
letters.desc: The filing endorses the ANOPR principle that large loads bear 100% of assigned network upgrade costs, and pushes FERC to extend that to all costs caused by large loads, both direct and indirect, so ratepayers do not subsidize interconnection.
quotes: the State Entities are encouraged by the ANOPR's inclusion of ratepayer protection principles, including that "[l]oad and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned."

this rulemaking must include provisions that mitigate the risk of ratepayer subsidization of large load interconnection, including by ensuring that the above cost assignment principle includes a robust assessment that assigns all costs caused by large loads (both direct and indirect) to those same large load customers.

letters.desc: Microsoft accepts responsibility for its share of network-upgrade costs and supports transparent calculation so neighbors and the local community do not subsidize it. Where up-front-funded upgrades broadly benefit other system users, it favors a crediting mechanism, possibly modeled on generator-only interconnection credits.
quotes: Microsoft supports the work of utilities and regulators to make sure these costs are transparently calculated and assigned to it and the other customers who benefit from those capital investments. This work helps ensure that Microsoft’s neighbors and the local community do not pay for Microsoft’s share of the costs.

If the network upgrades (with costs paid for up-front by the interconnecting loads they are assigned to) are providing broad benefits to other system users—for example, if another industrial customer benefits from the same infrastructure —Microsoft believes it would be fair to use a crediting mechanism or other arrangement that would capture the reliability and economic value those network upgrades provide other electricity consumers.
One such approach may be similar to the crediting mechanisms used for interconnecting generator-only facilities.

letters.org: National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners
letters.desc: NARUC supports specifying that large load customers are responsible for 100 percent of upgrade costs, consistent with the cost causation principle.
quotes: Any proposed rule should specify that large load customers are responsible for 100% of the upgrade costs consistent with the cost causation principle.

letters.org: National Association of State Utility Consumer Advocates
letters.desc: NASUCA and allied consumer advocates support assigning 100% of network upgrade costs to the large loads that cause them, with no crediting mechanism. Credit mechanisms are seen as directly contrary to cost causation principles and as a means of shifting costs onto existing ratepayers.
quotes: this rulemaking must include provisions that mitigate the risk of ratepayer subsidization of large load interconnection
making data centers responsible for 100% of the costs of network upgrades they are assigned
a crediting mechanism is directly contrary to this protective mechanism because it relieves large loads from a portion of the costs of network upgrades.

letters.desc: NRECA strongly supports the principle that interconnecting large loads pay all network upgrade costs they cause, grounded in cost-causation and beneficiary-pays doctrine. Crediting should not be a uniform requirement, and utilities need flexibility on financial security. Cooperative capital structures make absorbing these costs particularly risky for existing members.
quotes: NRECA supports this principle as essential to keep rates affordable to other consumers and to protect them from cost shifting and stranded costs.
It stands to reason that the costs resulting from the direct access of large loads to the transmission grid should be borne by those who benefit from that access.

Interconnecting loads should be responsible for the costs of these network upgrades to ensure that other transmission customers do not bear stranded transmission costs for upgrades made to accommodate the interconnection of a large load that fails to materialize, does not take service in the anticipated volume or peak and off-peak patterns, or ceases operation.

utilities should have the flexibility to determine the appropriate financial security for such upgrades. The capital structure of most cooperatives, which, by design, runs lean on the debt/equity ratio, limits their ability to absorb the costs of the build-out associated with large loads in ways that do not unfairly burden other customers.
NRECA does not support a hard-and-fast rule on whether such a crediting mechanism is appropriate for large-load interconnections.

letters.org: Natural Resource Defense CouncilSustainable FERC ProjectClean Air Task Force ,Coalition for Affordable Utility Services and Energy Efficie ,EARTHJUSTICE ,ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND ,MONTANA ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION CENTER ,Sierra Club ,Southern Environmental Law Center ,
letters.desc: Large loads must pay 100% of the network upgrade costs they cause. The filers oppose any default crediting mechanism and insist that a utility seeking cost sharing for a particular upgrade must affirmatively prove the degree and identity of broader beneficiaries.
quotes: new large loads should be responsible for the costs they cause, and it would be unjust and unreasonable for the costs caused by new large loads to be shifted to existing consumers who did not cause those costs and who receive no, or trivial, benefits from the infrastructure developed to serve new large loads.

FERC should not adopt a default crediting mechanism to offset the costs of network upgrades required for large load interconnection. Again, because large loads are the sole or primary beneficiaries of the network upgrades required for their interconnection, it is appropriate for them to bear 100% of the costs of those upgrades.

letters.desc: NRG supports requiring interconnecting loads to fund 100 percent of network upgrade costs. It criticizes state revenue-guarantee approaches as failing to match guaranteed payments to actual upgrade cost requirements, which can either force existing customers to subsidize large loads or overcharge the loads themselves.
quotes: NRG strongly supports the Secretary's proposed eighth principle for large load interconnection: that "load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through the interconnection studies."

many state-regulated utilities seek a "revenue guarantee" based on embedded cost rates multiplied by the MW-demand of the data center for some length of time.  Sometimes called "minimum commitments," this provision has been advertised as a policy approach that causes data centers to pay their fair share of grid costs, which may suggest alignment with the eighth principle announced in the ANOPR, but this is not an accurate understanding of the details of the "revenue guarantee" or "minimum commitments" provisions which have so far been adopted by state commissions.

the transmission and distribution revenues guaranteed by a large load addition customer could be substantially more or substantially less the revenue requirement of the transmission and distribution investments that would not have been needed but for that customers' large load addition.

letters.org: Office of the Ohio Consumers' Counsel
letters.desc: OCC calls for an express prohibition on transmission credits, rate-based recovery, and regional cost allocation for large-load upgrade facilities, citing the risk that credits evolve into broad cost socialization and violate established cost causation case law.
quotes: such "credits" frequently evolve into generalized cost socialization—resulting in rate impacts borne by retail residential customers who do not benefit from the facilities being built.
Prohibit the use of transmission credits, rate-based recovery, or regional cost allocation mechanisms for interstate transmission facilities built primarily to serve large private loads

Ensure that transmission cost recovery aligns with current cost causation and cost allocation principles developed in Illinois Commerce Commission v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 2009) (ICC I) ("FERC is not authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.")
The Commission should affirm that no interconnection right or transmission upgrade will be granted unless the applicant bears 100% of the costs of interconnection-related costs.

letters.desc: ODEC strongly supports assigning 100% of network upgrade costs to the large loads that cause them, including both PJM Supplemental and Baseline RTEP projects. It also invites FERC to reexamine whether the Order 2003 crediting mechanism's "but for" test should apply to large-load upgrades at all.
quotes: this pursuit must be achieved without shifting unjust or unreasonable costs onto incumbent native load customers, particularly residential and small commercial ratepayers

The Commission should use this opportunity to take measures to ensure that the costs associated with accommodating these extraordinary new demands are borne by the new large loads driving them, consistent with cost-causation principles.
ODEC strongly supports allocating 100 percent of the interconnection costs to the large load and hybrid facilities assigned to them through the interconnection studies.
ODEC would support the Commission revisiting the applicability of the "but for" test from Order No. 2003 regarding the network upgrades needed to serve new large loads.

letters.desc: ODEC supports direct assignment of transmission upgrade costs to the large load causing them, and acknowledges FERC may need to consider whether a pool-based cost allocation covering broader network maintenance is also appropriate.
quotes: all costs associated with transmission upgrades and facilities caused by the large load interconnection must be allocated to the large load or, as necessary, the FERC-jurisdictional entity serving the large loads.

letters.desc: OpenAI supports letting commercially-ready loads fund and voluntarily build required network upgrades, subject to appropriate protections, when doing so accelerates interconnection.
quotes: OpenAIsupportsallowing,subjecttoappropriateprotections,commercially-readylarge loadstofundandvoluntarilyconstructrequirednetworkupgradesidentifiedbythetransmission provider,whendoingsowillacceleratetheinterconnection.

letters.desc: Paces supports giving constrained, non-power-ready locations slower timelines paired with clearer upgrade cost expectations, so that speculative projects at costly sites face transparent signals rather than joining the same queue as well-sited loads.
quotes: Permit slower timelines and clearer upgrade expectations for heavily constrained, non-power-ready locations.

letters.desc: JCA support direct assignment of network upgrade costs to large load customers through the Expansion Rate Policy, citing the cost causation principle, the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and the risks that current structures impose on native load. They favor this approach over both rolled-in treatment and incremental-only pricing.
quotes: The Commission should adopt the Expansion Rate Policy set forth in the FirstEnergy Whitepaper for incremental network upgrades, because it (1) presents a practical and legally acceptable pathway to ensure just and reasonable rates for all consumers in light of the rapid onset of voluminous interconnections of hyperscale data center large loads to the interstate transmission system; and (2) would be the lynchpin to effectuating the Ratepayer Protection Pledge as to interstate transmission wires charges for incremental network upgrades, especially for network upgrades built as part of Supplemental Projects.

hyperscale data center developers promised to "pay for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades required to service their data centers, including adequate network upgrade costs to ensure that these expenses are not passed on to the ordinary household."

Such an agreement would align well with the principle of cost causation and avoid having existing customers subsidize the costs of network facilities from which existing customers derive no benefit commensurate to the benefits that large load interconnecting customers derive.

current cost structures require existing customers to unduly bear short-term costs and long-term costs and risks due to (1) the unique load ramping characteristics of data center large loads, and (2) the execution of electric service agreements that fall far short of the life of installed transmission assets.

Immense opportunity exists to benefit existing transmission customers through large load customers' paying their share of embedded costs transmission rates, offsetting already high transmission rates.

the new large load customer may monopolize the incremental transmission capacity needed to serve them, meaning that the new pathway for electricity that ought to provide reliability and operational benefits is consumed by the large load customer's interconnection.

The Commission should require transmission owners to adopt a line-by-line incremental pricing mechanism for the expansion facilities necessary to interconnect and serve new large load customers and ensure that those customers still contribute to the embedded cost of the high voltage transmission grid.
The most critical component is that the cost of the facilities would be depreciated over the life of the contract.
The JCA submit support for the Expansion Rate Policy as it applies at the local level for Supplemental Projects.

letters.org: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer AdvocateDelaware Division of the Public Advocate
letters.desc: The filers endorse 100% cost responsibility for network upgrades assigned to large loads with no crediting mechanism, and advocate for a but-for causation test to ensure all upgrade costs driven by the large load are directly assigned rather than rolled into network rates.
quotes: The Joint Consumer Advocates agree that load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades assigned to them through the interconnection studies and that these costs should not be offset through a crediting mechanism. Such a mechanism risks other ratepayers paying for the network upgrades that are the responsibility of the load and hybrid facilities.

The Joint Consumer Advocates fully support revisiting a 'but-for' test when determining which costs should be paid 100% by the large load customer, as opposed to a general benefits test, because but for the large load, the transmission owner would not have incurred the costs to upgrade the network facilities to serve that customer and the upgrades would not have been put into service without the interconnection of the large load addition.

letters.org: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer AdvocateDelaware Division of the Public AdvocateIllinois Office of Attorney General ,
letters.desc: The filers urge FERC to assign 100% of network upgrade costs to the large load or hybrid facility that caused them, using a but-for causation test or a higher-of policy, with no crediting mechanism. They argue the current Mobile-Sierra review of individually negotiated agreements leaves existing customers exposed to mounting cumulative transmission cost increases.
quotes: large load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrade assigned to them through the interconnection studies and that these costs should not be offset through a crediting mechanism.

FERC should revisit a 'but-for' test when determining which costs should be paid 100% by the large load customers, similar to the test traditionally used by FERC for cost allocation for the interconnection of generators.

Without cost allocation reform, existing customers will face mounting transmission costs due to the cumulative effect of a patchwork of individually negotiated interconnection agreements, reviewed under a Mobile-Sierra standard, which comprise a significant portion of current grid usage.

letters.org: PSEG CompaniesPSEG Energy Resources & Trade LLCPSEG Power LLC ,Public Service Electric and Gas Company ,
letters.desc: PSEG proposes a two-track approach: front-of-meter upgrade costs should be rolled into transmission rates and shared by all customers (because they provide system-wide benefit), while upgrade costs for co-located arrangements should be directly assigned to those arrangements (because they do not use the transmission system).
quotes: network upgrades to accommodate load interconnections in front of the meter should be allocated to all transmission customers, including large load additions.
network upgrades required by co-location load arrangements should continue to be directly assigned to the co-location arrangements.

letters.desc: RWECE agrees with AEP that network upgrade cost uncertainty is a core problem driving speculative interconnection requests and impeding timely project completion. The entry fee concept and the near-term crediting mechanism are both framed as ways to reduce that uncertainty.
quotes: RWECE supports such an "entry fee" concept for its potential to provide certainty to project developers, both load and hybrid facilities ("LAHF") and generation, and avoid projects which seek to identify low-cost interconnection locations but are rarely constructed, as AEP describes.

solutions, including the crediting mechanism methodology identified in Principle #8 of the ANOPR, and which RWECE supported in its initial comments, can and should be implemented much faster than four years to meet the objective of this acceleration initiative.
For the longer term, the crediting mechanism should be replaced with an "entry fee" concept, which provides certainty and reduced risks for LAHF and generation participants.

letters.desc: Shell Energy argues that large loads should access existing network upgrade crediting mechanisms on the same terms as other customers, and that existing generators entering bilateral co-location deals should not face punitive network upgrade cost assignments.
quotes: Shell Energy does not support existing generation having discriminatory and punitive provisions that it must pay for network upgrades for engaging in a bilateral capacity sale.

Large loads and hybrid/co-located load and generation customers covered by this ANOPR should qualify for either of these existing crediting mechanisms (as load or as generation) for network upgrades they fund; a sufficient record would need to be established on why large loads are differently situated enough to justify discriminatory treatment under tariff provisions applicable to other new generation and new load customers.

letters.desc: SEIA agrees that loads triggering network upgrades should pay for them, consistent with Commission precedent. When load and generation are studied together, the Commission must require transmission providers to use transparent, standardized criteria to assign cost responsibility between the two.
quotes: As a general principle, SEIA agrees that if a large load interconnection request triggers a network upgrade, then that large load should pay for the upgrade.

The Commission should therefore require transmission providers to develop transparent, standardized criteria for determining cost responsibility in cases where both large-load interconnections and generation projects contribute to the same transmission constraints.

letters.org: Southern Environmental Law CenterAppalachian VoicesNorth Carolina Sustainable Energy Association ,South Carolina Coastal Conservation League ,Southern Alliance for Clean Energy ,
letters.desc: The filers call for a default rule requiring large loads to bear 100 percent of network upgrade costs they cause, with shared cost recovery available only when the load can demonstrate the upgrade resolves a pre-existing need and provides non-trivial benefits to existing customers. They also support extending the Option to Build to large load interconnection customers.
quotes: the Commission may find that existing practices that broadly allocate the costs of network upgrades caused by large load interconnections are unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory because they neither account for the unique transmission needs created by large load interconnections nor allocate costs roughly commensurate with benefits.
the Commission should adopt a default policy whereby large loads pay 100 percent of the costs for transmission upgrades required for their interconnections.
The Commission should allow interconnection customers to exercise the Option to Build and initially fund network upgrades.

letters.org: Southern Environmental Law CenterNorth Carolina Sustainable Energy AssociationAppalachian Voices ,Coastal Conservation League ,Southern Alliance for Clean Energy ,
letters.desc: The filers support directly assigning 100 percent of large load-caused network upgrade costs to those loads and keeping those costs out of rate base. They argue existing state reforms have not achieved this, and that FERC's cost causation obligations require it to act. They also point to a participant funding model from generator interconnection as a ready template.
quotes: Broadly spreading the costs of upgrades meant to integrate and benefit massive loads will overburden existing customers and further incentivize the piecemeal grid expansion that the Commission has found to be unjust and unreasonable.
Directly assigning the costs of large load-caused network upgrades and sequestering them from the broader rate base would accomplish this necessary goal.
none of the aforementioned state-level reforms have required large loads to pay the full cost of transmission upgrades they cause or otherwise insulate existing customers from their impact.

Transmission-owning utilities in the Southeast and their national representatives urge the Commission to retain its longstanding rolled-in rate policy for network upgrades caused by large load interconnections.

those rate structures may have made sense when relatively linear, organic load growth caused modest incremental upgrades, but they were not designed for enormous and fast-paced infusions of transmission investment dedicated to serving a relatively small number of large customers.
the Commission should directly assign the costs of network upgrades to the large loads that cause them using a similar model to participant funding for generator interconnection.

the Commission can and must find here that directly assigning the costs of network upgrades to large loads is necessary to address the unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential cost allocation practices identified in this proceeding.

letters.desc: SMECO supports requiring large loads and hybrid facilities to bear 100% of network upgrade costs assigned through interconnection studies via a federal framework analogous to Contribution in Aid of Construction.
quotes: SMECO supports a federal construct and framework in the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff that would directly assign costs associated with upgrades to the electric transmission system caused by a large load facility directly to the large load facility (or group of large load facilities) assigned through the interconnection studies.

A framework that would directly assign costs associated with upgrades to the electric transmission system caused by a large load facility - akin to a customer Contribution in Aid of Construction ("CIAC") at the wholesale level or Federal CIAC - would also entail the new large load paying network service thru the applicable network service rate once access to the grid is achieved by paying for the appurtenant necessary upgrade.

letters.org: Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group
letters.desc: Under HILL and CPP, load and hybrid facilities are responsible for assigned upgrade costs, but SPP reduces those costs by identifying Planned Interconnection Locations where capacity is pre-built. The filer supports this approach as superior to a generic cost-assignment rule.
quotes: under CPP and HILL framework, as well as the pending CHILLS framework, load and hybrid facilities will be responsible for the cost of upgrades.  SPP, however, takes an additional step by actually reducing the need for upgrades through its identification of Planned Interconnection Locations.

letters.desc: Terraflux agrees that interconnection customers should finance 100% of assigned network upgrade costs but prefers a direct cash reimbursement mechanism over crediting through transmission expenses.
quotes: We agree with the eighth principle's assertion that 100% of assigned network upgrades costs should be financed by the interconnection customer, however a liquid reimbursement mechanism is a cleaner and simpler approach than reimbursement crediting via transmission expenses.

letters.desc: TBA recommends that non-firm loads be exempted from upgrade costs allocated on the basis of peak contributions they do not make, aligning cost responsibility with actual system use during non-peak hours.
quotes: customers with non-firm withdrawal rights do not impose the same peak-driven infrastructure needs as firm network integration transmission service ("NITS") customers
the Commission should require that non-firm loads not be assigned costs for upgrades based on hours in which they are contractually barred from taking service

letters.desc: Tract supports crediting load customers for network upgrade costs when other customers use those upgrades, with credits continuing until 100% cost recovery rather than ending after a fixed period.
quotes: To the extent any network upgrades are assigned through interconnection studies to load or hybrid facilities, such costs should be offset through a crediting mechanism based on the actual usage of those upgrades by other networked customers.

letters.desc: TAPS supports requiring large loads to pay 100% of assigned network upgrade costs upfront. Any crediting mechanism must be designed to prevent cost shifts to other customers and must account for the unique risk that a data center fails to sustain the demand level for which upgrades were built. The existing generator crediting model is not appropriate.
quotes: TAPS supports holding Qualifying Large Load and Hybrid Facilities responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned. Principle 8 is key to addressing one of the most important challenges raised by large data centers and other similar loads: that, if rolled into wholesale transmission rates, the substantial costs of transmission upgrades needed to serve these unique loads gets borne by other customers
the Commission cannot achieve this goal by merely copying the existing crediting mechanisms used for different purposes in the different context of generator interconnections.
any crediting mechanism must account for the unique risks and characteristics of large data center loads to protect other customers.

letters.desc: TAPS supports holding large loads fully responsible for the network upgrade costs they cause, calling it the most protective approach for other wholesale customers. TAPS also rejects WIRES's narrow two-option reading of the "and" pricing policy, arguing FERC can modify that policy or use a crediting mechanism that requires upfront payment while returning credits when demand is sustained.
quotes: If that large load fails to achieve and sustain demand at the level for which these network upgrades were built, the costs of the upgrades will be allocated based on load ratio shares that do not reflect the addition of a large load (whose demand projections triggered the upgrades) to the peak load of the LSE serving that large load.

Holding large loads responsible for the costs of network upgrades they cause, as contemplated in the ANOPR, is the most protective of other wholesale transmission customers paying Commission-jurisdictional rates.

WIRES uses faulty assumptions in analyzing the narrow cost-shifting issue it does address. WIRES claims are based on the assumption that the Commission's existing "and" pricing policy requires an upfront determination that large loads pay only (1) the incremental costs of network upgrades they cause, or (2) rolled-in transmission rates.

The Commission is not restricted to completely exempting large loads from ongoing transmission charges if it holds large loads initially responsible for the full costs of the network upgrades they cause.
The Commission's ability to address this major, new challenge need not be hamstrung by past policy developed to address very different issues.

Under that mechanism, the large load would pay the upfront cost of any network upgrades, but it would have the opportunity to be credited back that full amount, so long as its transmission usage over time is sufficient to cover the costs.

This ensures that the large load pays the higher of either incremental costs or rolled-in transmission rates, mitigating the stranded cost risks to other wholesale customers if the large load fails to maintain a level of demand sufficient to justify the cost of the network upgrades caused by the large load.

letters.desc: The Coalition argues maintaining dispatchable storage energy during peaks can dramatically reduce or eliminate the network upgrade costs that would otherwise be required to serve large loads.
quotes: Enabling large loads to avoid drawing from the grid by maintaining dispatchable energy during peak demand events—when transmission constraints are most salient—can dramatically reduce or eliminate the need for network upgrades that would otherwise require years of study and construction (as well as sizeable costs) to accommodate.

letters.desc: UCS documents a structural gap in which transmission upgrade costs driven by large loads flow through FERC formula rates into state retail rate cases, where they are spread across all customers rather than assigned to the causing customer class. The filing uses PJM data to illustrate the scale and calls Principle 8 a correct application of cost causation to close this gap.
quotes: Costs for transmission connections and network extensions required by new large loads have already added over $4 billion to the ratebase of utilities in 2024 from construction in just seven states.
The existing rules and practices allow the worst outcome: the rapidly rising costs for data centers' needs are spread across all the utilities' customers.

Under existing practices the revenues from new large load customers are recognized for the largest customer class, but the costs caused by those customers are allocated to all customers. This is not the application of the 'Bonbright' cost-causation principle that is so often cited in utility cost allocation debates.

this proposed Principle of assigning costs for all upgrades identified in the interconnection studies for large loads will address a regulatory gap and correctly apply the widely cited principle of cost causation to significant costs presently misallocated to all consumers.

letters.desc: The filers want FERC rules that place transmission upgrade costs squarely on large load customers rather than distributing them across the existing ratepayer base under current allocation practices.
quotes: Rate payers in markets with data centers have been subject to higher utility bills as the costs of transmission upgrades and expansions are distributed based on current allocation practices.
Safeguards to prevent large load customers from shifting interconnection or transmission upgrade costs onto existing rate payers.

letters.desc: Vantage accepts full responsibility for network upgrade costs caused by its interconnections and supports Principle 8's cost assignment approach. Vantage also seeks a rate crediting mechanism to prevent double recovery through both upgrade cost assignment and system average embedded transmission charges.
quotes: Vantage emphasizes that the specific principles and reforms concerning (1) hybrid interconnecting data center facilities supported in whole or in part by dedicated generating facilities (Principles 3 and 5), (2) expedited interconnection study procedures (Principle 7), (3) cost allocation for interconnection-related network upgrades (Principle 8), and (4) a fair and structured transition that respects existing rights (Principle 13) are of greatest importance.

The recommendation of Proposed ANOPR Principle 8 that large loads should be fully responsible for assigned network upgrades attributable to their interconnection accords fully with Vantage's commitment to absorb the full cost of upgrades required by its projects.

a transmission rate crediting mechanism is appropriate to ensure full compliance with the Commission's 'higher of' transmission pricing principle by ensuring that the data center customer is not allocated the full cost of network upgrades caused by its interconnection plus the system average embedded cost of transmission.

letters.desc: VEIR asks that cost-allocation rules acknowledge when advanced conductors reduce or eliminate the need for network upgrades, and that crediting mechanisms exist for non-traditional upgrade paths.
quotes: Ensure cost-allocation frameworks acknowledge when interconnection upgrades are mitigated or avoided entirely by advanced conductors while allowing crediting for non-traditional upgrade paths.

letters.desc: Verrus supports letting flexible loads nominate curtailment commitments in the study process to avoid, reduce, or defer network upgrade assignments, lowering interconnection costs and accelerating timelines.
quotes: Flexible loads that meet this definition should also be allowed to nominate operational flexibility commitments in the study process that allow the Transmission Provider to avoid, reduce, or defer network upgrades, thereby accelerating interconnection and reducing system costs.

letters.desc: Vistra supports the principle that new-build co-location minimizes the need for network upgrades by reducing net transmission use, and endorses charging co-located facilities based on net injection and withdrawal rights to correctly size upgrade requirements.
quotes: the Commission should make clear that co-location arrangements involving new load and new generation should minimize the need for network upgrades, minimize line losses, and create efficiencies in equipment, land use, permitting, and siting.

letters.desc: The filers contend ATTs can deploy in 18 to 36 months using existing ROW at lower cost than traditional upgrades, and that DLR alone could eliminate a $400 million upgrade triggered by a 1% overload. They frame mandatory ATT evaluation as the key mechanism for keeping interconnection costs just and reasonable.
quotes: ATTs can rapidly increase the grid's capacity in 18-36 months using existing infrastructure and rights-of-way ("ROW") providing fast solutions to unlock new grid capacity while also being a bridge to bring new large loads on more quickly while new network transmission upgrades are built.

"Because the benefits of the enumerated alternative transmission technologies identified above are present across all interconnection processes, regardless of the size of the interconnection request, we find that the failure to evaluate the enumerated alternative transmission technologies results in both the pro forma LGIP and pro forma SGIP being unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential."

Order No. 2023 found that ATTs "can be deployed more quickly to be used as network upgrades in place of, and at a lower cost than, traditional network upgrades," and highlighted the numerous benefits commenters stated ATTs can provide including, "resolving thermal overloads and avoiding voltage collapse, allowing for better use of the existing transmission system, improving reliability, and reducing interconnection request withdrawals, restudies, and overall interconnection delays."

One generation developer was assessed for a $400 million upgrade based on a 1% projected line overload. Depending on the utility's rating methodology, DLR has potential to increase the capacity of that line by more than 1% in all conceivable weather scenarios.

letters.desc: WIRES argues large load customers should pay for the upgrades and expansions necessary to interconnect and serve them, over both the short and long term, under existing transmission pricing policy.
quotes: the Commission should require that its overall existing transmission service pricing policy is applicable to new large loads.  That is, as they do today, such load customers should pay for the cost of transmission service with such costs reflecting the upgrades and expansions necessary to interconnect and serve such large load customers, over both the short and long term.

letters.desc: ATC opposes blanket direct assignment of all network upgrade costs, arguing most upgrades benefit all customers and should be socialized. ATC supports direct assignment only for facilities exclusively attributable to the new load (analogous to generator TOIFs) and for specialty equipment required because the load fails to meet performance criteria.
quotes: ATC maintains that such costs should be socialized because these network upgrades ultimately benefit all customers.
ATC recommends that the Commission narrowly tailor direct assignment of interconnection facility costs to those that can be directly attributed to and likely exclusively used by the new load.

the Commission should consider requiring new loads to bear 100% of the costs for facilities necessitated by their characteristics that do not conform with planning and interconnection criteria addressing behavior such as oscillation, ramp, and low-voltage ride-through.

ATC encourages the Commission to incorporate transmission owner initial-funding in any future requirements related to load interconnection procedures.  Without the option to self-fund load interconnection projects, a customer's option to build would present several concerns to ATC.

letters.desc: CAISO supports the 100% cost responsibility principle for loads but asks for explicit guidance on how to allocate costs for hybrid facilities where generator and load upgrade needs cannot be cleanly separated.
quotes: the CAISO requests that any final rule provide clear guidance on cost responsibility for hybrid facilities: Separating which network upgrades were required by a generator and which network upgrades were required by a co-located large load is impractical, if at all possible for some types of upgrades.

letters.desc: The CPUC supports ratepayer protection in upgrade cost recovery but argues that the five-year generator reimbursement period is too short for load customers. Because load may ramp more slowly and is not backed by resource adequacy obligations, a longer payback period is needed to avoid stranded investment risk for ratepayers.
quotes: For any cost offsets (i.e., reimbursements to large load customers) for transmission network upgrades, it is imperative that they occur over a period sufficient to ensure that risks to other ratepayers associated with the failure of generation to timely materialize, and costs borne while load ramps up, are fully mitigated.

the five years over which payback to generators occurs is likely too short a period to ensure that load will develop and be sustained.  Any reimbursement to load customers for their upfront investment in load energization upgrade costs would likely need to occur over longer than five years to ensure protection of other ratepayers.

letters.desc: DEC accepts that large loads are responsible for their assigned upgrade costs, but requests phased or partial cost responsibility for facilities that demonstrably reduce grid stress through curtailment or on-site generation.
quotes: The Commission should affirm DOE's principle that large loads and hybrid facilities remain responsible for their assigned upgrade costs but clarify that those demonstrating verifiable curtailment or on-site generation may qualify for phased or partial cost responsibility.
Aligning cost responsibility with actual system impact ensures fair treatment, promotes investment in flexible technologies, and encourages efficient infrastructure development.

letters.desc: DPN accepts that loads bear their assigned network upgrade costs but wants those costs credited back over the PPA, capped at half the PPA length, and flags open questions about infrastructure ownership and tax credits.
quotes: the upgrade costs need to be credited back to the facility over the course the power purchase agreement (PPA) length. The maximum duration for issuing the credit should be 50% of the PPA length.

letters.desc: Eolian presents the Matta Grid example to show that excluding load from generator studies inflated network upgrade cost assignments by over $100 million, and argues that reformed study processes would reduce unjustified upgrade costs.
quotes: PJM's Phase II study results assigned $158 million in network upgrade costs to Matta Grid, largely driven by a grid constraint 25 miles from both the Matta Grid project and the proposed Amazon data center. A Timmons Group study that Eolian commissioned demonstrated that, had PJM included even a very conservative 150 MW of the 770 MW of Amazon load in its Phase II study for Transition Cycle 1, the study results would have shown over $100 million less in system reinforcements assigned to the Matta Grid project.

letters.desc: The KCC agrees large loads should pay upgrade costs assigned through interconnection studies, but argues the bigger problem is cost allocation for regional transmission expansion plans that states cannot fully address. It supports the goal of protecting traditional load from cost shifts but says the ANOPR's focus on interconnection-study upgrades is too narrow.
quotes: The minimum bill calculation includes payment of a reasonable allocation of all transmission costs incurred by the retail utility to serve retail customers, including network upgrades constructed as a result of interconnection studies or other regional transmission expansion plans.

the focus on cost allocation within interconnection studies is misplaced. The larger issue is the cost increases and potential cost shifts associated with regional transmission expansion plans, which states do not have authority to fully address.
there is currently no mechanism under federal statutes or regulations that require projected loads to commit to pay for the regional projects ahead of building those projects

letters.desc: Longroad acknowledges the ANOPR's 100% cost assignment to interconnecting customers but argues that a crediting mechanism is essential. Without reimbursement, unnecessarily high upgrade costs will deter both generation and large load, repeating the failures of the current process.
quotes: Upgrade costs for generation that are unnecessarily costly have prevented generation from being built, which delays service to large loads.

Longroad urges the Commission to adopt a crediting mechanism. Load and generation would provide backstop security or funds to enable the interconnecting transmission owner to build any required network upgrades following what the Commission adopted in Order No. 2003, and then the load and generation would be reimbursed via credits or cash.

Transmission customers and load clearly benefit as the Commission found in Order No. 2003 and related cases because of the integrated nature of the network upgrades. Reimbursement effectuates that reality.

letters.org: New York Transmission OwnersCentral Hudson Gas & Electric CorporationNew York Power Authority ,New York State Electric & Gas Corp. and Rochester Gas and El ,Niagara Mohawk d/b/a/ National Grid ,Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. and Orange and ,Long Island Power Authority ,
letters.desc: The NYTOs support the principle that customers driving new upgrade costs should bear those costs, and that transmission owners must recover a regulated return on assets they build and operate. They oppose a blanket direct-assignment rule that would conflict with state retail ratemaking frameworks, and ask that any federal cost framework preserve regional flexibility and respect state authority over upgrade cost allocation.
quotes: the Commission should focus any cost allocation and option to build rules on those large load customers likely requiring the most transmission improvements (e.g., at 100 MW).

customers that drive new costs should bear the economic weight of the facilities dedicated to their use; Transmission Owners should have the right to recover their costs plus a regulated return when they construct, own, and operate assets upon which the system relies; and federal actions should not upend established allocation frameworks or compel Transmission Owners to operate facilities without full cost-of-service recovery, including an authorized return.

A nationwide rule that presumes all upgrade costs must be directly assigned to the interconnecting load customer would not account for these distinctions and could conflict with existing state-jurisdictional approaches to resource adequacy, retail ratemaking, and customer protection.

letters.desc: SPP supports requiring large load customers to bear 100% of assigned upgrade costs but asks that any federal crediting mechanism align with its existing ILTCR framework under Attachment Z2 and Attachment J. SPP also asks that cost allocation decisions respect the SPP Regional State Committee's established governance role.
quotes: If the Commission determines in a final rule that large load customers should only be charged for transmission service based on their withdrawal rights, SPP urges the Commission to consider all costs incurred by granting this type of transmission service to ensure that costs are allocated appropriately so that transmission owners are held harmless by the usage.

SPP requests that any final rule adopted based on this Proposed ANOPR provide the RSC with the opportunity to provide significant input into how network upgrade costs will be allocated within SPP as it relates to the interconnection of large loads.
SPP requests that any crediting mechanism allowed under any proposed rule in this docket be consistent with Attachment Z2 and Attachment J of the SPP Tariff.

letters.desc: WIRES presents quantitative evidence that directly assigning 100 percent of network upgrade costs to large loads, when paired with exemption from NITS charges under the anti-double-charging rule, shifts substantial transmission costs onto other retail customers. The filing supports the goal of making large loads pay their fair share but opposes a sole direct-assignment framework that produces unintended cost shifts.
quotes: The Whitepaper sets forth an analysis of the ANOPR's proposal to allocate 100 percent of network upgrade costs to large load customers and illustrates the potential for unintended cost shifts to retail customers under certain implementation scenarios.
directly assigning network upgrade costs to large load customers can lead to significant transmission cost shifts away from large load customers onto other retail customers.

A prohibition on 'and' pricing might allow the same large load customers, having paid for their network upgrades, to argue that they should be exempt from the rates that fund the ongoing development, maintenance, and operation of the broader transmission system, called Network Integration Transmission Service ('NITS') charges.

Our core finding is that direct assignment of network upgrade costs, with accompanying excusal from paying NITS charges, results in significant transmission cost shifts away from the large load customers and onto other customers.
over time, these cost shifts could amount to $33-47 billion in present value terms for just the volume of large loads expected to be developed in PJM from 2025-2030.

if the Commission were to implement in PJM a sole direct assignment policy for network upgrades associated with large loads interconnecting in the 2025-2030 period, the average PJM customer could experience an approximately 8-11 percent increase in the transmission portion of their retail electricity bill, or about $23-33 more per year in 2026 dollars.

it shows that when large loads pay only for their required network upgrades and do not contribute to the embedded system costs or the future costs required to maintain system reliability for all customers, including themselves, those costs are shifted onto other customers.
This approach creates a problematic cost shift from an equity and policy standpoint. Furthermore, such rate treatment ignores the reality that the transmission system is an evolving investment.

establishing a crediting mechanism for large load customers would effectively reimburse them for any network upgrade costs that they were responsible for. Once they have been fully reimbursed, they would presumably then be responsible for NITS obligations like any other customers.

letters.desc: ATC believes direct assignment of 100% of network upgrade costs to the load is too broad and complex. It should be confined to facilities exclusively attributable to the new load, and any framework must ensure TOs receive initial funding and a fair rate of return.
quotes: ATC, along with several stakeholders, supports continued allocation of network upgrade costs to all transmission customers that benefit from the enhanced transmission system, consistent with Commission precedent.
ATC believes such direct assignment would be highly complex and likely result in disputes, confusion, and delays.
Direct assignment should be narrowly tailored to facilities exclusively attributable to and used by new loads to help contain costs and maintain alignment with cost-causation principles.
